title: NASA Roman Space Telescope Set to Launch August 30, Targeting 100,000 New Worlds
excerpt: The next-generation observatory will survey the cosmos with a field of view 200 times wider than Hubble, arriving at its launch site nine months ahead of schedule.
body:
• NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is set to launch on August 30, 2026, aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Kennedy Space Center — about nine months ahead of its original schedule.
  • The observatory is expected to discover around 100,000 exoplanets in a single mission, more than every telescope in history combined, while mapping billions of galaxies to study dark energy and dark matter.
  • Roman will join the James Webb Space Telescope at the Sun-Earth L2 point, roughly one million miles from Earth, for a planned five-year primary mission.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is on track to launch on August 30 at 7:26 a.m. EDT from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. The flagship astrophysics mission, which completed construction in November 2025 and arrived at the launch site on June 21, is running about nine months ahead of its original schedule.

Named after Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief astronomer who championed the Hubble Space Telescope in the 1960s, the observatory carries a 2.4-meter primary mirror — the same diameter as Hubble's — but with a field of view 200 times larger. That wider lens will allow Roman to conduct rapid, sweeping surveys of the universe that no existing telescope can match.

A Census of New Worlds

The telescope's most ambitious goal is an unprecedented survey of exoplanets. Scientists expect Roman to detect approximately 100,000 planets beyond our solar system through gravitational microlensing — a technique that measures how a planet's gravity bends and magnifies the light of a background star. That tally would exceed the combined discoveries of every telescope in the history of astronomy, according to Space Daily.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=gMaOxuw5wnE

"The Roman Space Telescope is going to be transformative for transient science," said Mitchell Karmen, a graduate student at Johns Hopkins University and National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellow. "Thanks to Roman's high sensitivity, we can find multiple tidal disruption events out to greater distances and earlier cosmic times than ever before."

Dark Energy, Dark Matter, and Black Holes

Beyond exoplanets, Roman will tackle some of the deepest questions in cosmology. Its Wide Field Instrument will map the distribution and shapes of billions of galaxies across enormous volumes of space to measure the effects of dark energy — the mysterious force accelerating the expansion of the universe. The same surveys will trace the invisible scaffolding of dark matter that shapes cosmic structure.

New research published in The Astrophysical Journal suggests Roman will also detect supermassive black holes that shred and consume stars — events known as tidal disruption events — out to distances corresponding to 11 billion years ago. These observations could reveal how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew in the young universe.

How Roman Compares to Hubble and Webb

While the James Webb Space Telescope excels at deep, narrow-field observations in infrared light, Roman is built for breadth. A single Roman image will cover an area of sky equivalent to about 100 Hubble images at comparable resolution. This makes it ideal for surveys that require mapping large swaths of the cosmos quickly — work that would take Hubble centuries to complete.

Roman also carries a Coronagraph Instrument, a technology demonstration designed to block starlight so that faint nearby exoplanets and planet-forming disks can be studied directly. If successful, it will be a precursor to future missions aimed at imaging Earth-like planets around other stars.

Launch Preparations

Engineers at Kennedy Space Center have been working through final pre-launch checks since the observatory arrived in June. Technicians placed the telescope onto a specialized work platform called the Pantheon, powered up its systems for checkouts, and began testing its six solar array panels. The remaining steps include inspecting insulation and thermal blankets, testing propellant tanks, loading approximately 290 gallons of hydrazine fuel, and encapsulating the telescope inside the Falcon Heavy payload fairing.

After launch, Roman will travel to the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2, roughly one million miles from Earth, where it will orbit alongside JWST. The L2 point provides a stable, unobstructed view of the universe while keeping the telescope far enough from Earth to avoid interference. Following a multi-month commissioning phase, Roman is expected to begin science operations and will conduct its planned five-year primary mission from that vantage point.
